intrepid

in-TREP-id -- stress on the second syllable, TREP. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intrepid is fearless or adventurous.

The intrepid rescue pilot flew into the canyon in a crosswind that had turned back two other crews.

Example

An intrepid twelve-year-old signs up to give the very first speech at the school assembly -- not because she is a natural on stage, but because somebody has to go first and nobody else will.

Fearless, willing to walk toward the thing others avoid -- and always admiring. Intrepid is not the same as reckless: an intrepid person meets real danger on purpose and with open eyes, while a reckless one never stops to look at all.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fearless: Fearless means the fear simply is not there -- danger does not register at all. Intrepid people are braver in a harder way: they feel the danger, weigh it with open eyes, and walk toward it anyway. Fearless describes an absence; intrepid describes a choice.

daring: Daring admires bold risk-taking, and it often loves the thrill more than the judgment -- a daring stunt can be a foolish one. Intrepid is steadier praise: an intrepid person accepts real danger deliberately and for a purpose, never just for the rush.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

timid: lacking courage; easily frightened

fearful: full of fear; afraid to act

Where it sits · how lasting and unshakable the courage is

valiant → intrepid → dauntless

valiant vs. intrepid: Valiant praises the courage inside a single act -- a valiant stand at one bridge -- while intrepid describes a settled character that keeps choosing the dangerous road, day after day.

dauntless vs. intrepid: Dauntless goes one step past intrepid: an intrepid traveler feels the fear and goes anyway, while a dauntless one cannot be discouraged at all, by any setback or any warning.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-: not (Latin in-)

root — trepid-: fearful, trembling (Latin trepidus 'alarmed, trembling')

Put it together: Intrepid is this unit's prefix in- ('not') on Latin trepidus ('trembling with fear'), so an intrepid person is literally 'not trembling.' Be honest about the limit: 'trepid' is not a word you can use on its own in modern English, which makes this decomposition likely rather than airtight -- but the root is alive and well in trepidation.

Use the root in a new word: trepidation: She mentioned her trepidation just once, in the last line of the interview.

Root Check

Word Choice

Intrepid is a compliment, and it keeps good company: an intrepid explorer, an intrepid reporter, an intrepid rescuer. Keep it clear of reckless, which is a criticism -- an intrepid climber studies the route and then climbs it, while a reckless one climbs without ever looking at it.
